beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new, it's a title

beats.trigger: Hire three agents to search. Three more to decide.
beats.got: Agents are described as hires, which makes me ask who they replace. The filesystem as a meeting room is a nice image I only half follow.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: nothing new, a list of homework links. 'Helper agents' appears before anyone has explained it.

beats.trigger: **Analyze** handoff failures: hidden conflicts, clashing dialects, beige averaging
beats.got: I will build some agents and look at where they go wrong. 'Dialects' and 'beige averaging' are jargon I can't decode yet. Nothing here says what it means for my people.

beats.trigger: What do you expect will get lost between them?
beats.got: Handing work between agents can lose things, which is a fair question. It's the same as handing work between people.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Sending to Slack changes another system.
beats.got: An agent writes the message, a human approves it, and only then does it send. I could explain that boundary to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: Push back hard when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I ask the agent for the one thing that unlocks everything else, then keep pushing. That is useful for the pricing-change onboarding problem. It's still a tool step, though.

beats.trigger: Paste each retriever prompt and confirm its short list quickly.
beats.got: Four windows and five prompts to paste, and a lot of juggling. I don't see who in my team would do this or own it afterwards.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if it is right; that is expected.
beats.got: Three helpers with different stances produce a synthesis I can't verify yet. For people decisions that makes me uneasy.

beats.trigger: Your team will ask: *when do I split, and how?*
beats.got: The lecture is about when to use several agents instead of one. 'My team' is mentioned, which helps a bit.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: One agent per recurring workflow is a unit I know from HR processes, such as onboarding or the monthly metrics run.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: Start with one agent and split only when you must. This is the sober, understated advice I trust.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Splitting by access means one agent never sees data it shouldn't. That is how I'd think about employee data and who gets to see it.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough"
beats.got: More agents isn't more rigour. It's the same lesson as 'more meetings is not more alignment'.

beats.trigger: Three stances give you a spread of views, and a spread is not an answer.
beats.got: Without a framework the AI summarises all views equally. A framework forces a choice. I could take that to the leadership team: ask which frame we hand our people to decide with.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: Before splitting, ask whether one prompt would do the same job. It repeats the earlier point.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: There are two ways to split, sessions or helpers. I think I follow, but 'Phase 1 and Phase 2' and 'long-lived state' are jargon.

beats.trigger: Other agents are part of the tool surface: one agent can call a different stance, source zone, or working style.
beats.got: nothing new. 'Tool surface' is jargon and the slide mostly repeats the previous one.

beats.trigger: Splitting creates handoffs, and handoffs are where work goes wrong.
beats.got: Handoffs are where work goes wrong, in agents as in teams. That is a familiar org-design point, and it's also the first slide I'd show to HR partners.

beats.trigger: A whole module showed multi-agent works. Don't apply it to everything.
beats.got: A caution against overdoing it. I appreciate the understatement.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in recognisable ways, and the most worrying one is confidence right before a failure.

beats.trigger: This prompt is long. Make your own variant.
beats.got: Ask the agent to diagnose where its own system went wrong. The prompt is long, and I'm not sure I would trust an agent to audit itself.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."
beats.got: When something fails, check the sources, the processing or the boundary. For risky steps, have the agent propose and a human decide.

beats.trigger: then rewrites the root instructions file in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent updates its own rules file after reviewing the session. It's another paste-a-prompt step.

beats.trigger: The audit reads how your agents handed work to each other; it does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: Nothing in the process checks whether the answer is true. That is honest, and it's also why I wouldn't act on it for people decisions without a human check.

beats.trigger: Push back where it's wrong
beats.got: I read the summary and argue with it where it's off.

beats.trigger: Keep the unease about the synthesized briefing as an open question. Do not fix it today.
beats.got: The course asks me to carry the doubt forward instead of resolving it. That is unusual, and I respect it.

beats.trigger: Memory is a working artefact, sharpened by what it bumps into.
beats.got: Optional homework to test the memory files. I'll skip it.

beats.trigger: Split only where agents can't be one: access, dialect, stance.
beats.got: Split only for access, dialect or stance. It's a handy three-line summary.

beats.trigger: [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: nothing new, more reading links.

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agent risk sits on top of normal security. The words are dense, but data and security are where my DPO and works council come in.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: The question to carry to the next module is what the worst thing is that an agent could do with its access. For employee data that is a real question for me, and I haven't asked the DPO yet.

beats.trigger: You're close to an agent system that cracks your crux.
beats.got: Keep building on my own problem until the next module. It's a bit optimistic, since mine isn't close to cracking anything.

take_homes: Start with one agent. Split only when the agents need different access, speak different dialects, or must disagree. Handoffs between agents are where it breaks, just like between people.
Several views are not an answer. A framework forces a choice, and I can take that idea to my leadership team.
Nothing in the process checks that the result is true, and access matters. Before employee data goes near this, I need the works council and the DPO.

monday.move: Ask my DPO and one HR business partner what employee data an agent may touch. Then sketch a one-agent version of my weekly people-metrics summary that proposes and never sends.
monday.who: Me, my DPO and one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday morning, in my one-to-one with the DPO
monday.stop_condition: The DPO says employee data in this tool needs the works council first. Then I stop and start that conversation.
monday.blocker: Works council and DPO sign-off for employee data in an AI tool. I haven't asked yet.

misconception.why: The module never talks about roles, hiring or headcount. It treats agents as hires that do the work, so I still expect headcount to be the first question. I still think the question is which roles go, and nothing here changed that.

one_line: Sensible, sober advice on when to use more than one agent, and the access point was useful to me. But it was all about the tools, and nobody said what it means for the people doing the work.
